title: Bracket Every Dot in an Address
statement:
Security reports often write IP addresses so that they cannot be clicked or pasted by accident: every dot . becomes [.].

Given a valid IPv4 address address (four numbers from 0 to 255 joined by dots), return it with every dot replaced by [.]. Nothing else changes.

examples.why: All three dots are wrapped. The digits stay exactly as they were.
Short numbers do not matter; it is still three dots.
The longest possible address, still three replacements.

constraints: address is a valid IPv4 address
hints: You only ever change one kind of character. What happens to every other character?
Build a new string: copy each character, but write [.] when you meet a dot.
Most languages have a replace-all for this. In JavaScript, replace with a plain string only replaces the first match.

explain.intuition:
Strings are immutable in JavaScript and Python, so you build a new one. Walk the address, copy each character, and emit [.] instead of each dot. The output is the input length plus 2 for every dot.

A built-in replace-all does the same walk for you. The trap is JavaScript's "a.b".replace(".", "[.]"), which replaces only the first dot.
steps: Start an empty list of output pieces.
For each character: push [.] if it is a dot, otherwise push the character.
Join the pieces and return the result.
pitfalls: Using String.prototype.replace with a string pattern, which changes only the first dot.
Building a regex from "." without escaping: /./g matches every character, not just dots.

solutions.title: Copy character by character
solutions.idea: Walk the string and emit [.] for each dot, the character itself otherwise.

solutions.title: Split and join
solutions.idea: Split on the dots and join the four parts back with [.] between them.

followups: Do the reverse: turn a bracketed address back into a normal one.
Also handle IPv6, which uses colons. What changes?
